tools.description:
Launch a new agent to handle complex, multi-step tasks. Each agent type has specific capabilities and tools available to it.

Available agent types are listed in messages from the system in the conversation.

When using the Agent tool, specify a subagent_type to select an agent: `"fork"` forks yourself (the fork inherits your full conversation context and always runs on your model — a `model` override is ignored); any other type — or omitting it — starts a fresh agent (general-purpose by default).

## When to use

A fresh agent costs more than it looks. It knows only what you put in the prompt, and you see only the summary it sends back — both handoffs drop detail, and neither of you can tell what the other missed. You can't watch it work, only wait or cancel. Its mistakes come back in the same confident register as its findings, and an agent handed your hypothesis tends to return it confirmed. Several at once spend tokens in a burst the user didn't ask for. Weigh those tokens against the accuracy they buy: the user pays for agents you did not need, and pays again for work you redo because you skipped one.

Reach for this when you have independent work to run in parallel, when the user asks for a side quest that shouldn't block your main thread, or when answering would mean reading across several files — delegate that and you keep the conclusion, not the file dumps.

Do the work yourself when it is a handful of tool calls or a lookup whose target you already know; don't delegate a check you could run inline. Delegate review only when you want a read that isn't anchored on yours — then give it the code, not your conclusion. Once you've delegated something, don't also run it yourself; wait for the result. When in doubt, don't spawn.

When you do spawn one, brief it like the peer it is: state the goal and what you have already ruled out, point it at the files and docs worth reading instead of retyping them, and keep the scope explicit and narrow. That brief is the only context it will have, so it is your first lever on every cost above — and if you cannot write a clear one, you do not understand the task well enough to hand it off.

A fork runs in the background and keeps its tool output out of your context. If you are the fork, execute directly — don't re-delegate. Subagents run in the background; you'll be notified when one completes. Never fabricate or predict a pending agent's results — the notification is never something you write yourself; if the user asks before it arrives, say it's still running.

- The agent's final report is not shown to the user — relay what matters.
- Use SendMessage with the agent's ID or name to continue a previously spawned agent with its context intact; a new Agent call starts fresh (except subagent_type: "fork", which inherits your context).
- Each agent type's model, reasoning effort, and tools come from its definition (`.claude/agents/*.md` frontmatter or SDK `agents`).

{"body":"## Problem Statement

The user keeps household money in a plain-text ledger file and is tired of spreadsheets. They want a small tool that reads that file and shows where the money went. It has to work as an importable Python library and as a terminal command.

## Solution

A pure-stdlib Python (>=3.9) package called `pennywise`. It is installable with `pip install .`, which gives both `import pennywise` and a `pennywise` console script. A parser turns the ledger text into typed entries and reports the exact line of any mistake. Aggregation helpers cover balance, per-category totals, per-month totals and filtering. An argparse CLI offers `balance`, `summary`, `list`, `add` and `export`, with `--json` output and clearly defined exit codes.

## User Stories

1. As a user, I run `pennywise balance house.txt` and see my total, e.g. `1457.50`.
2. As a user, I run `pennywise summary house.txt [--by category|month]` and see one sorted line per group.
3. As a user, I run `pennywise list house.txt --category groceries --since 2024-03-01 --until 2024-03-31` and see matching entries, oldest first.
4. As a user, I run `pennywise add house.txt 2024-03-07 groceries -12.30 "corner shop"` to append an entry safely.
5. As a user, I run `pennywise export house.txt` to get CSV.
6. As a user, I add `--json` to balance/summary/list to feed other tools.
7. As a user, I pass `-` as FILE to read the ledger from stdin.
8. As a scripter, I `import pennywise` and use `parse`, `balance`, `by_category`, `by_month`, `filter_entries`, `ParseError`.
9. As a user with a typo in my file, I get told exactly which line is wrong (exit 1, stderr only).

## Implementation Decisions

**Layout:** `pyproject.toml` (setuptools build backend, `requires-python = ">=3.9"`, no runtime dependencies, `[project.scripts] pennywise = "pennywise.cli:main"`). Package in `src/pennywise/`:
- `__init__.py` re-exports the public API: `Entry`, `ParseError`, `parse`, `balance`, `by_category`, `by_month`, `filter_entries`.
- `ledger.py` holds the model, parser, aggregations and formatting helpers.
- `cli.py` holds argparse and `main(argv=None) -> int`.
- `__main__.py` makes `python -m pennywise` work.
Tests live in `tests/` and use stdlib `unittest`, so `python -m unittest discover -s tests` works. pytest may also run them.

**Entry:** a frozen dataclass `Entry(date: datetime.date, category: str, amount: Decimal, note: str = "")`.

**Parsing rules** (`parse(text) -> list[Entry]`):
- Split lines with `str.splitlines()`, so LF and CRLF both work. Line numbers are 1-based and count every physical line.
- A line that is empty or whitespace-only is blank and skipped. A line whose first non-whitespace character is `#` is a comment and skipped.
- Otherwise strip the line at both ends and match `^(\S+)[ \t]+(\S+)[ \t]+(\S+)(?:[ \t]+(.*))?$`. The note is group 4, kept exactly as written (internal whitespace preserved), or `""` when absent. Fewer than 3 fields is an error.
- Date: must match `^\d{4}-\d{2}-\d{2}$` and be a real calendar date (`2024-02-30` is an error).
- Category: any non-whitespace token, stored with `.lower()`.
- Amount: must match `^[+-]?\d+(\.\d{1,2})?$`, then `Decimal(token)`. Rejected: `12.505`, `1,000.00`, `abc`, `.5`, `12.`, `1e3`.
- On error, raise `ParseError(line, message)`. It subclasses `ValueError` and has a `.line` int attribute. `str(err)` starts with `line N: ` followed by a reason (e.g. `line 4: invalid amount '12.505'`).

**Aggregations:**
- `balance(entries)` returns `sum(..., Decimal("0"))`.
- `by_category` and `by_month` return dicts of Decimal totals. Month keys look like `"YYYY-MM"`.
- `filter_entries(entries, category=None, since=None, until=None)` matches category case-insensitively, keeps both date bounds inclusive and preserves input order. `None` means no filter on that field.

**Formatting:** amounts are always shown with 2 decimals via `quantize(Decimal("0.01"))`. A zero result never prints as `-0.00`; normalise negative zero to `0.00`.

**CLI** (argparse, `prog="pennywise"`):
- `balance FILE [--json]` prints `1457.50`, or with `--json` prints `{"balance": "1457.50"}`.
- `summary FILE [--by category|month] [--json]`. The default is category. Each line is `name  total`, separated by two spaces and sorted by name. JSON is an object with keys in sorted order and string amounts.
- `list FILE [--category C] [--since DATE] [--until DATE] [--json]`. Entries are stable-sorted by date (same-day entries keep file order). Each line is `DATE CATEGORY AMOUNT[ NOTE]`. JSON is an array of `{"date","category","amount","note"}` (note is `""` when absent).
- `add FILE DATE CATEGORY AMOUNT [NOTE]` builds the line `DATE CATEGORY AMOUNT [NOTE]` and validates it with the same parser. A note containing a newline, an invalid date or an invalid amount is refused: exit 1, a stderr message, and the file is not touched. If valid, append the canonical line (lower-case category, 2-decimal amount, note trimmed). If the existing file is non-empty and does not end in a newline, insert a newline first. Create the file if it is missing. Print the canonical line, formatted exactly like `list`. `add` never reads stdin; `-` is not special for it. `add` does not validate the existing file contents.
- `export FILE [--format csv]` writes CSV with the `csv` module, header `date,category,amount,note`, rows in `list` order, 2-decimal amounts and `\n` line terminators. `csv` is the only allowed format (argparse `choices`).
- `-` as FILE reads `sys.stdin` (for balance/summary/list/export).
- Files are read as UTF-8.
- Exit codes: 0 means success. 1 means a ParseError in the ledger or an invalid `add` entry; print `pennywise: <file>: line N: <reason>` (or `pennywise: invalid entry: <reason>` for add) on stderr and nothing on stdout. 2 means the file cannot be read (missing, directory, permission, decode error), shown as a `pennywise: cannot read <file>: ...` message on stderr, or the command line is wrong: no command, unknown command, bad `--by`/`--format` value, or an invalid `--since`/`--until` date (argparse `type=` that raises `ArgumentTypeError`, so argparse exits 2).
- `main()` returns the int and the console script uses it as the exit status. Output always ends in a newline.

## Testing Decisions

- Unit tests for the parser cover each valid/invalid amount example from the request, invalid dates (`2024-02-30`, `2024-13-01`, `24-03-01`), comment and blank handling, note whitespace preservation, tabs as separators, CRLF, case-folding, and the ParseError line/`ValueError`/message.
- Unit tests for balance (including empty → `Decimal("0")`), by_category, by_month and filter_entries (inclusive bounds, case-insensitive, order kept).
- CLI tests call `cli.main([...])` and capture stdout/stderr. They check every command, `--json` shapes, stdin `-`, list sort stability, add (creation, newline handling, refusal leaves file byte-identical) and every exit-code case.
- One end-to-end smoke test runs `python -m pennywise` in a subprocess.
- Stdlib `unittest` only.

# pennywise

Read a plain-text household ledger and see where the money went. Pure Python (3.9+), standard library only.

    pip install .

installs the `pennywise` package and the `pennywise` command.

## Ledger format

    # household, March
    2024-03-01 salary 2500.00 March pay
    2024-03-02 groceries -42.50 weekly shop

    2024-03-05 Rent -900

Each line: `DATE CATEGORY AMOUNT [NOTE]`, separated by spaces or tabs. Dates are `YYYY-MM-DD`, categories are
case-insensitive (shown lower case), amounts have at most two decimals (`12`, `+12.5`, `-0.99`). Blank lines and
lines starting with `#` are ignored. Any other mistake is reported with its line number.

    import pennywise
    entries = pennywise.parse(open("house.txt").read())
    print(pennywise.balance(entries))

    pennywise list FILE [--category C] [--since DATE] [--until DATE] [--json]
    pennywise add FILE DATE CATEGORY AMOUNT [NOTE]
    pennywise export FILE [--format csv]
